topic: multi-agent systems; process verification; verifier-guided search
status: bounded full-text synthesis from one sampled ICML 2026 study spanning six MAS frameworks; external replication not performed
claim: Process-level verification is not a generally reliable quality gate: in MAS-ProVe, its effects depend on verifier type, context, granularity, architecture and task, with both gains and regressions. The useful research target is a conditional policy that predicts when verification helps, not a blanket assumption that intermediate judging improves MAS.
positive_evidence: MAS-ProVe reports gains in some AIME24/25, GAIA, HumanEval and GPQA configurations; e.g., Debate with GPT-5-mini judge improves from 74.13% to 81.11% on AIME24.
LLM judges outperform RM/PRM in 24 of 36 reported configurations; several best judge/context configurations improve stability on solvable hard questions.
counterevidence: Table 1 includes numerous verifier/granularity/model settings below their no-verifier baselines; agent-call vs iteration-level preference changes by architecture/task.
On AIME24/25 (30 items each) and GAIA information extraction (103), the main comparisons average three runs; search samples N=3 candidates and uses greedy reranking.

The paper finds limited resurrection of questions that fail across baseline trials; GAIA includes substantial task-specific tool and operator adaptation, and HumanEval uses a different generator setup.

sources.version: v2 / ICML 2026 Regular per arXiv record
sources.sections: Secs. 3-4, Tables 1-5; Appendix A.1-A.2 and B

falsifiable_test: On frozen held-out tasks, compare no verifier, judge, RM and PRM while fixing generator/verifier versions, candidate count, prompt/context, architecture, compute and seed schedule. Estimate treatment effects by task difficulty and architecture, including negative regressions, token cost, and zero-success recovery. The conditional-heuristic claim weakens if one verifier/granularity yields stable positive gains across held-out task families and budgets; it strengthens if a preregistered context/difficulty policy beats both the global default and no-verifier control.
limitations: One paper, three-run main comparisons and small AIME test sets; no independent reproduction in this audit. Frameworks and tasks are heterogeneous and some were adapted for the study. Do not infer a field-wide average treatment effect.

topic: multi-agent memory; structured collaboration state; scientific ideation
status: bounded comparison of two sampled 2026 full texts plus one abstract-level counterpoint; cross-paper headline scores are not pooled
claim: Persistent structured state has promising but task-bounded evidence when the task exposes an editable object: typed claim/proposal state can outperform aggregation or text-centric baselines on specific conflict-resolution and ideation benchmarks. The evidence does not support a universal memory benefit or forced reconciliation of every conflict.
positive_evidence: LatticeMind reports 0.97 (73/75) on label-blind ConflictBank vs 0.61 majority vote, with a same-evidence, neutral-source-name protocol.

EIG reports 7.41 vs 6.95 for its strongest automatic baseline on a fixed 512-group ideation subset; in a blinded 24-group expert study, overall quality is 4.01 vs 3.50 and average rank 1.64 vs 2.92, with paired intervals excluding zero for those summary outcomes.
Both papers include component ablations favoring explicit structured state/controller operations.
counterevidence: LatticeMind's four secondary planning sets have n=10-15 and include a TravelPlanner regression; its real-repository replay bridge covers two trajectories. Its main benchmark addresses credibility conflicts, while coordination/irreducible conflict is not validated.

EIG's human ratings cover only 24 groups; rubric confidence intervals include zero for novelty, feasibility and context adherence. Its controller is trained on heuristic labels, and its evaluation is ideation-only, not implementation or scientific outcome.

TANGLE (arXiv:2608.13921) frames some memory conflicts as genuinely underdetermined and reports that extraction can erase conflict-bearing relations; only its arXiv abstract was consulted here, so this is a scope counterpoint rather than a full-text-verified replication.

sources.sections: Secs. 3-4; Appendices F, I, J and L

sources.version: abstract only; not full-text audited in this batch
sources.sections: arXiv abstract: TANGLE benchmark and unresolved-conflict framing

falsifiable_test: Factorial comparison of transcript-only, typed persistent graph/memory and answer aggregation under matched backbone/evidence/token budget, crossed with resolvable vs genuinely underdetermined conflicts. Measure answer accuracy, provenance, calibration, unsupported supersession, conflict retention and clarification seeking on blinded held-out items, plus downstream proposal implementation outcomes. The structured-state claim weakens if gains vanish on held-out conflicts or induce more false forced updates; it strengthens if gains replicate without erasing ambiguity and predict downstream success.
limitations: Three sources from one recent frame cell; one source is abstract-only; benchmark families, metrics and sample sizes differ, so score magnitudes cannot be pooled. This is not a novelty or prevalence claim and no proposed factorial experiment was run.

topic: AI for science; research ideation; evaluation validity
status: bounded inference from one sampled full-text ideation study and external primary-source reports; no proposal-execution experiment run
claim: High ideation benchmark or reviewer scores are not evidence that generated scientific proposals will be implemented successfully or produce useful empirical results. EIG explicitly evaluates the proposal stage only; broader end-to-end systems evaluate execution separately, while a 2025 primary-source study frames an ideation-execution novelty/utility trade-off.
positive_evidence: EIG's benchmark and blinded human results agree on stronger proposal ratings, supporting a scoped claim about benchmark-defined ideation quality.

CodeScientist (Findings of ACL 2025) reports hundreds of automated experiments and subjects 19 discoveries to external review, code review and replication attempts; six were judged at least minimally sound and incrementally novel, illustrating the need for execution/replication evidence beyond proposal ratings.
counterevidence: EIG's 24-group human study is still an ideation judgment task and its authors explicitly state implementation survival is a separate future-work question.
Schapiro et al. (2025) report a persistent novelty-utility trade-off in their creativity task; this is related evidence, not a direct evaluation of EIG or all scientific domains.
CodeScientist studies a constrained software/agent domain and its judged discoveries are not a universal estimate of scientific idea success.

sources.sections: Sec. 4 and Appendix L: ideation evaluation and scope limitation

sources.title: CodeScientist: End-to-End Semi-Automated Scientific Discovery with Code-based Experimentation

sources.sections: Abstract: novelty-utility and ideation-execution trade-off claim

falsifiable_test: For a blinded held-out proposal set, preregister feasibility criteria, implement proposals under matched compute/time, and compare pre-execution benchmark/expert scores with successful reproduction, effect size, and resource cost. Report calibration by domain and idea type. The separation claim weakens if pre-execution scores consistently predict implementation and positive empirical outcomes across domains; it strengthens if highly rated proposals fail systematically or novelty trades off with utility under controlled budgets.
limitations: EIG full text was audited; CodeScientist and Schapiro et al. were checked at primary-source abstract/landing-page level only in this batch. Findings are not an estimate of general scientific success rates.
